extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, students of fiction, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using pictorial description vs dramatic action in novel-writing: how to prepare scenes, introduce romance or climax, handle time, and shape characters so extraordinary events feel credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed romance in a background of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: If a fabulous or romantic tale can be 'firmly embedded in a background of truth', its falsity may be disguised and the whole book may pass for a scene of the human comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realistic, detailed setting and social truth to make marvels believable; beware that if the romance is too gaudy or the realism too starkly true, the contrast will make the romance 'staringly false' (Balzac's difficulty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead gradually into romantic intrigue through populated scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead into romantic or fabulous action 'gradually, through well-populated scenes of character and humour', so the world is actual and its air familiar by the time the plot thickens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give ample margin before the climax (as in Dickens/Bleak House): use a broad stream of diversified life that 'moves slowly' so the reader accepts the later extraordinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare the scene so it vouches for the violent drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce violent or abrupt drama only into a scene 'already prepared to vouch for it' — a scene so alive and queer that almost anything might happen there naturally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the pictorial background attest to the action; the picture's effect can be used as an attestation of the subsequent drama, reducing the need for contrived justification when the climax occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a broad pictured life as reserve of force for the drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a distributed, pictured scene — a world 'that could easily include' both ordinary figures and romantic ones — so the drama draws strength from the surrounding life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Populate the background with characters and incidents that furnish an 'appropriate scene' and 'favouring background' even if they take no specific part in the main action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer immediate scene/action and dialogue over large general narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Present life 'in the form of scenic action' — hold to the immediate scene and let character be shown by what people 'talked and behaved' in a certain hour, on a certain spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for dramatic immediacy, show characters through scenes and dialogue rather than summarizing; this may require sharper, more formulaic rendering of minor characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharp, economical characterization for scene-driven fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: When the picture is translated into action, characters must be 'crystallize[d] and formulate[d] very sharply' because their opportunities are limited to a few scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept the expedient of labelling or giving characters a recurring trick/phrase so they are effective in narrow bounds; failure of some sketches is expected, but many succeed brilliantly with this economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose presentation method to suit subject (first-person vs third-person picture)
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of presentation (e.g., first person) has different effects depending on subject: it can be 'the first step towards dramatization' or can 'tone' a drama into a pictured impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a story benefits from being presented as someone's narrative (to dramatize or to filter the picture) and use that viewpoint to enhance either the drama or the pictorial impression as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build setting from precise, minute detail when the author fully possesses the image
rubrics_metrics.description: Some writers (Balzac) imagine people inseparable from 'their streets and houses and rooms', giving minute inventories ('the doorway is approached, the passage leads to the staircase') as essential preliminaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you truly know the place in your thought, reproduce it 'inch by inch, fact by fact' to create a firm, telling impression. If you do not possess such an image, this mechanical accumulation of detail will ring false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere mechanical detail if you cannot inhabit the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'impressionist' writer who is aware of the effect of a scene rather than the scene itself must not attempt Balzac's method; otherwise the account will be a mechanical sum of details making no image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match descriptive method to your imaginative knowledge: either own the scene completely and describe fully, or use suggestion and side-lights rather than exhaustive inventory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the opening picture to secure the representation of time
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary pictured scene can 'include the representation of time', so that later the author may sum up years concisely ('Five years went by in this way') without losing the sense of protracted duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed habits, routines, and the character of everyday life in the picture so the accumulation and sameness of years are latent from the start, allowing time to be treated economically later.

rubrics_metrics.name: When material is slight but spans long time, choose pictorial externalization or internal elaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: If little happens externally but the story spans many years, a novelist can either (a) elaborate the character's inner life at length (telling it from within) or (b) prepare a comprehensive picture of the world so the passage of time is implied externally (Balzac's way).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the approach that suits the subject: if the protagonist lacks inner resonance, external pictorial method may preserve interest; if inner life is rich, an intimate, patient interior narrative may be preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the climax complete the organic whole and be free of unnecessary burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax's task is 'to complete, to add the touch that makes the book whole and organic' and it should not be distracted by matters that could have been settled earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design earlier stages to 'despatch' what would otherwise distract the climax; determine whether the climax should be pictorial (a slow impression) or a dramatic point (a single incident) and shape it accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save the climax from deliberate expatiation when the effect is pictorial
rubrics_metrics.description: For an essentially pictorial climax (e.g., the slow chill of Eugenie's hope), avoid hinging the book on a sudden discovery; the worst disappointments 'do not happen like that' but 'steal into a life'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the climax is an impression of change and decay requiring time, provide the long preparatory picture so a concise factual coda suffices rather than extended dramatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: For repetitious-progressive subjects, prepare a rich scene to be denuded step by step
rubrics_metrics.description: For stories that consist of repeated similar shocks growing in intensity (La Recherche de l'Absolu), amass in the opening picture an 'ample resource' — dignity, opulence, portraits, furniture — which can be visibly stripped away to renew and increase effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the material scene as a measurable ledger of decline: each recurrence of the effect gains force from the visible loss in the setting rather than fading by repetition.
